summary:
The Penal Code in force since 15 November 2022, a revision of the Spanish Criminal Code dating to the Francoist era, does not explicitly criminalise same-sex intimacy or gender diversity. Same-sex sexual activity is lawful and the age of consent is 18 regardless of gender or sexual orientation. Article 364(2) bars employment discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, the first provision in Equatoguinean law explicitly protecting lesbian, gay and bisexual people, and Law 1/2016 on the Protection of Personal Data (Articles 10 and 41) protects personal data on "sexual life" where it entails discrimination.

Enforcement does not follow the statute. Authorities continue to apply the 1954 Law on Vagrants and Criminals, which classifies homosexuality as an illness and normalises conversion practices. A 2020 Draft Law "Regulating Prostitution and the Rights of Homosexuals" would effectively criminalise same-sex conduct; its status is unresolved in the most recent source, an Outright International profile updated March 2026.

Three further instruments institutionalise discrimination: the Military Justice Code, a ministerial order concerning "immoral" activities, and a provincial regulation. Couples whose relationship the law reads as same-sex have no legal recognition and are not eligible for the protections available to opposite-sex couples.

Police and military personnel intervene in the spaces of assembly, expression and residence of lesbian women. In Bata, police have detained known lesbians collectively, on the stated ground that "lesbians are members of a sect", and have imposed collective punishment when a single lesbian is sought. The Synergía IHR report documenting these practices was published in 2024 and does not date the raids.

Transgender women have reported harassment and sexual violence while in police custody, and security forces have subjected LGBTQ+ people to sexual violence and discrimination in the military, jails and prison. School officials have reportedly denied transgender students access to some facilities, teachers have reportedly discriminated against and excluded LGBTQ+ girls, and academics and government employees can be ousted if perceived as not heterosexual. LGBTQ+ children are reported to be driven from their homes, with school dropout as a consequence.

Documented incidents include the 2014 detention of four men over a video found on a phone, after which they were made to explain their actions on national television; a lesbian couple in Añisok tied up at the police station, paraded through town with banners calling them witchcraft-practicing lesbians, photographed and shamed; and the August 2023 illegal detention by police of Trifonia Melibea Obono, founder of Somos Parte del Mundo, after her group submitted a report on torture and ill-treatment of LGBTQI+ people to the EU headquarters in Madrid, after which arrests and restrictions rose significantly. The most recent dated incident in this record is August 2023; no later dated instance is documented. ILGA reports that state intimidation of sexually diverse individuals persists, and that LGBTQ+ people are still detained and punished through public shaming despite the absence of an explicit prohibition.

The record documents rape used as a form of conversion practice, and the forcible impregnation of queer women in an attempt to make them heterosexual. LGBTQ+ women and transgender men are described as vulnerable to sexual violence in the military and from family members. Laws against rape are not effectively enforced: the source states that the crime is rarely reported, and that police and judicial officials may decline to act where the perpetrator has political connections or is a member of the police or military.

A local NGO identifies transgender children as especially vulnerable to commercial sexual exploitation, and minors generally are sexually exploited for commercial sex.

The US State Department's 2021 human-rights report found that same-sex conduct was not specifically criminalised, that LGBT persons faced societal stigma, and that no anti-discrimination protections existed. That snapshot predates the 2022 Penal Code and its employment provision.
tangentialFactors:
A stakeholder submission to Equatorial Guinea's fourth Universal Periodic Review, filed by Small Media, EG Justice, IPI and Digital Rights in Equatorial Guinea, documents restrictions on freedom of expression, digital rights and journalist safety. The submission frames these as the repressive environment that also constrains LGBT advocacy, so advocacy work carrying an LGBT label carries the same exposure as other dissent.

An analysis in Hispanic Studies Review (October 2025) of Trifonia Melibea Obono's 2019 novel "Yo no quería ser madre" reads the Equatoguinean social climate as one of compulsory heterosexuality and queer invisibility. This is literary and social-climate evidence rather than a legal finding.

The 2021 US State Department reporting places the absence of explicit criminalisation inside a wider context of general political repression, which is the same context in which the August 2023 detention of a LGBTI rights organiser occurred.
localsOnly:
Article 364(2) of the Penal Code gives residents a statutory bar on employment discrimination based on sexual orientation, and Law 1/2016 (Articles 10 and 41) gives a claim over personal data on "sexual life" where that data is used to cause discrimination. Neither instrument reaches the practices the record documents: academics and government employees ousted if perceived as not heterosexual, and teachers excluding LGBTQ+ girls from education.

Residents accused of homosexuality are still processed under the 1954 Law on Vagrants and Criminals, which treats homosexuality as an illness and normalises conversion practices. Three additional instruments institutionalise discrimination against residents: the Military Justice Code, a ministerial order on "immoral" activities, and a provincial regulation.

Residents in relationships the law reads as same-sex obtain no legal recognition and are excluded from the protections available to opposite-sex couples. LGBTQ+ residents are driven from the family home, a displacement that ends in school dropout.

Transgender residents face harassment and sexual violence in police custody, and LGBTQ+ residents face sexual violence and discrimination in the military, jails and prison. Rape is used as a conversion practice and queer women are forcibly impregnated; reporting of rape is rare, and police and judicial officials may decline to act where the perpetrator has political connections or belongs to the police or military. A local NGO identifies transgender children as especially vulnerable to commercial sexual exploitation.

Residents who advocate publicly face detention: the August 2023 arrest of the founder of Somos Parte del Mundo followed her organisation's submission of a report on torture and ill-treatment of LGBTQI+ people abroad, and arrests and restrictions rose significantly afterward.
outOfScopeNotes:
The status of the 2020 Draft Law "Regulating Prostitution and the Rights of Homosexuals" is unresolved. The most recent source, dated March 2026, states that its status is unclear, and no later instrument in the record resolves whether it has been enacted, withdrawn or remains pending.

Whether the 1954 Law on Vagrants and Criminals remains formally in force is not stated. Sources describe it as obsolete while documenting its continued application by authorities; the record does not contain a repeal date or a court decision on its validity.

The record contains no information on legal gender recognition documents, name or marker change, hormone access, medication or health services for trans residents. No source addresses entry, visa or airport-screening treatment of trans travellers to Equatorial Guinea.

Dates are missing for several documented harms: the police and military raids on lesbian assembly and residence spaces recorded by Synergía IHR, the collective detentions in Bata, and the parade of the lesbian couple in Añisok. Only the 2014 television confession incident and the August 2023 detention are dated.

No source provides trans-specific violence counts with population denominators, per-capita rates, or a ranking of Equatorial Guinea against other jurisdictions. The IRB-CISR country-information source yielded no usable finding on Equatorial Guinea.
